extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and planetary observers (telescopic observers and scientifically-interested readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and inferential criteria for interpreting telescopic observations of Mars (terminator projections, dark/blue-green areas, seasonal changes, and atmospheric phenomena) — aimed at distinguishing mountains, clouds, dust, water, and vegetation from visual evidence. Emphasizes methods, limits of detectability, and multi-opposition comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique-illumination (terminator) method for revealing relief
rubrics_metrics.description: When mountains or valleys chance to lie upon the boundary of light and darkness (the terminator) they make their presence evident through an indirect species of magnification, the elongate effect of oblique lighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the terminator/oblique lighting to detect relief: small elevations cast long shadows and peaks catch sunlight far from the illuminated surface, producing protracted profiles. Analogous terrestrial example: slant street lighting exaggerating surface irregularities. Best opportunity is near sunrise/sunset on the planet (terminator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative visibility limits for detectable elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: To see a peak on Mars by terminator effect requires high magnification; with power of 250–300 (or sometimes twice this), theoretical detectable heights reduce to something like 2,500 feet (with further allowance for atmospheric imperfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided scaling: in spheres of different diameters the distance out from the terminator for a given height is as the square root of the diameter. Compare lunar detectability (e.g., lunar peaks of 15,000 feet visible) to infer minimal detectable heights on Mars given aperture, magnification, and seeing; always increase theoretical limits to allow for atmospheric degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence (fixed-location) test to distinguish mountains from clouds
rubrics_metrics.description: A mountain cannot change its place. If a projection on the terminator does not recur in the same place when the same region is presented on the following night, it cannot be due to a mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observations of the same longitude/latitude as the planet rotates nightly. If the feature is not fixed in position and appearance across successive presentations of the same region, treat it as atmospheric (cloud/dust) rather than solid relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion and dissipation indicate atmospheric origin
rubrics_metrics.description: If the projection moves in position, shrinks, or dissipates over hours/days (e.g., was much smaller after 24 hours and disappeared later), then the cause is atmospheric (cloud) rather than a fixed geological peak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track temporal evolution: drifting, shrinking, and disappearance are diagnostic of clouds or dust-clouds. Mountains would not change size, move, or vanish on such short timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as diagnostic of cloud composition (vapor vs dust)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary vapor clouds are whitish; the observed Martian projection was tawny/ochre, 'of the tint exhibited by a cloud of dust', implying material of the soil rather than vapor tinted by sunrise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the hue of the projection to nearby regions similarly illuminated (e.g., Baltia showing whitish). If a projection retains a soil-like tint distinct from nearby illuminated zones, prefer dust-cloud interpretation. Consider illumination effects before concluding intrinsic color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached/island-like projection morphology as evidence of suspended matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasions where the projection forms an 'oval patch of light ... parted from [the terminator] by darkness to the extent of half the projection’s own width' (a detached islet of light) indicate a body suspended above the surface rather than a surface peak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note morphology: true peaks produce crescent coronets or profiles contiguous with the illuminated disk; fully detached illuminated patches separated by dark space are symptomatic of clouds or suspended dust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of specular reflection argues against seas
rubrics_metrics.description: If the dark areas were oceans, one might expect specular reflection (a burnished glare) of the Sun at a calculable point; this was never observed on Mars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for the predicted reflection point using physical ephemerides; failure to detect the specular glint is evidence against large liquid seas producing the dark patches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent linear markings indicate solid (non-marine) surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the dark areas was found to be traversed by permanent lines. 'Permanent lines cannot exist on bodies of water,' therefore these lines show the dark patches are not seas but solid terrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and map persistent linear features; permanence in place across observations is a strong criterion for solid topography (ridges, valleys, geological structures) rather than fluid surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal/temporal changes in area and tone as evidence for vegetation
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the blue-green regions' aspect from one opposition to another (changes of area and tone) and observed intra-year metamorphoses (e.g., Mare Erythraeum turning chocolate-brown ~60 days after southern winter solstice) suggest seasonal biological activity such as vegetation growth and senescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic time series (within a single Martian year and across oppositions) to correlate color/area changes with Martian seasons. Interpret fading, paling, or shifts in hue as consistent with seasonal vegetation cycles (greening and autumnal browning) if timing matches expected seasonal phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-balance and physical-plausibility test against aqueous explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative criticism shows the water hypothesis implausible: the observed changes would require removal of many feet of liquid over hundreds of thousands of miles (lowering levels by 5–20 feet across vast areas), with no feasible reservoir or atmospheric mechanism to account for the displaced water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply simple mass-balance reasoning: check whether hypothesized transfers of water are physically feasible given polar-cap states, extent of dark areas, and atmospheric capacity. If the numbers are implausible, favor non-marine explanations (vegetation, surface color change, dust) over wholesale changes in ocean extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for systematic, multi-opposition observation and careful comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection of change in the blue-green areas and other phenomena required persistent, assiduous observation from opposition to opposition and careful comparison of records (Schiaparelli's work exemplified this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent records (drawings, micrometer measures, photometric notes) across many nights and oppositions; subtle changes (tone, area) often elude detection without long-term, repeated observation and comparative tabulation.
